title: Speech Privacy in Buildings
research_question: To develop a comprehensive rating method for speech privacy in buildings that accounts for multiple acoustical factors, and to validate this method against observed occupant reactions in field case histories, improving upon existing average transmission loss (TL) and categorization schemes.

participants.description: Approximately 10-13 test subjects drawn from a business-office environment for laboratory experiments; 37 case histories representing about 400 pairs of spaces in different kinds of buildings (offices, hospitals, dormitories, motels) for field analysis.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated for lab subjects, case histories were documented from various buildings.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Simulated private-office environments in a laboratory setting, with an adjacent room for intruding speech. Various wall types (e.g., 'flat', 'limp', 200-cps, 640-cps, 2-kc critical frequency walls) were simulated using physical walls, spectrum-shaping 1/3-octave filters, and attenuators. Intruding speech was a shorthand-training recording played through a loudspeaker. Background noise was steady, consistent, and approximated an NC-35 contour, generated by a 2-channel tape recording of traffic and diffuser noise.

37 real-world building case histories, each representing a specific pair of spaces (e.g., private offices, hospital rooms, dormitories) with varying construction types (e.g., wire stud, metal lath plaster, wood part, gypsum block, gypsum board on studs) and environmental conditions (e.g., background noise levels, room sizes).

measures.instrument: Categorical rating scale (Extreme Dissatisfaction, Strong Dissatisfaction, Moderate Dissatisfaction, Mild Dissatisfaction, Apparent Satisfaction) based on interviews with owners and occupants.
Push-button response when intruding speech became 'bothersome' for 'normal' work (Test A) or 'confidential' work (Test B).
Calculated Articulation Index (AI), a weighted signal-to-noise ratio.
Measured in 1/3-octave bands for intruding speech and background noise.
Measured or advertised average TL values of isolating walls.
Measured NR values of isolating walls.
Measured octave-band levels in various spaces.
Categorized as conversational, raised, or loud voice.
Floor area, room volume, reverberation time (T), sound absorbing area (Sā).

findings.antecedent: Average transmission loss (av TL) of isolating wall (e.g., 35 db)
findings.mechanism: Average TL alone does not capture the complexity of speech privacy perception.
findings.quote: an average transmission loss of 35 db is not the demarcation between satisfaction and dissatisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Average transmission loss (av TL) of isolating wall (>= 35 db) in office cases
findings.mechanism: Other factors beyond average TL contribute to privacy perception.
findings.quote: In 7 of the 11 office cases where the transmission loss was 35 db or above, the occupants experienced significant dissatisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Average transmission loss (av TL) of isolating wall (< 35 db) in office cases
findings.mechanism: Other factors beyond average TL contribute to privacy perception.
findings.quote: in 5 of the 9 office cases where the occupants were apparently satisfied with the privacy, the average transmission loss was less than 35 db.

findings.antecedent: Steady background noise level (submerging speech peaks)
findings.mechanism: Masking of speech sounds by background noise.
findings.quote: The intelligibility of intruding speech is destroyed when the speech peaks are submerged in steady background noise

findings.antecedent: Increase in background noise level
findings.mechanism: Masking effect is equivalent to increased transmission loss.
findings.quote: an increase in the background level has the same effect on intelligibility as an increase in the transmission loss.

findings.antecedent: Variation in background noise levels (30 dB or more)
findings.consequent: Effectiveness of a given isolating structure (for speech privacy)
findings.mechanism: Background noise contributes to masking, thus its variation impacts the perceived effectiveness of a barrier.
findings.quote: we would expect a comparable variation in the 'effectiveness' of a given isolating structure built in these different locations.

findings.antecedent: Talker-room size (e.g., small 6 ft x 8 ft office vs. large 40 ft x 40 ft classroom)
findings.consequent: Reverberant speech levels (assuming constant speech power)
findings.mechanism: Larger rooms with constant speech power result in higher reverberant speech levels.
findings.quote: the corresponding range in reverberant speech levels is 15 db.

findings.antecedent: Ratio of wall area to listener-room floor area (e.g., 2:1 vs. 1:2)
findings.mechanism: Geometric factors influence the amount of sound transmitted.
findings.quote: the corresponding variation in transmitted levels is 6 db.

findings.antecedent: Speech effort (raised voice vs. conversational, loud voice vs. conversational)
findings.mechanism: Increased vocal effort directly increases speech sound power.
findings.quote: the sound levels for a 'raised voice' are about 6 db higher than those for conversational speech; a 'loud voice' is about 12 db higher.

findings.antecedent: Privacy requirement (confidential vs. freedom from distraction/normal)
findings.mechanism: Higher privacy needs lead to a desire for lower intelligibility of intruding speech.
findings.quote: the more critical occupants desired a fairly low intelligibility of intruding speech when their work was confidential

findings.antecedent: Privacy requirement (confidential vs. normal)
findings.consequent: Difference in speech signal to background noise ratio
findings.mechanism: A 6-dB difference in signal-to-noise ratio was observed between normal and confidential privacy requirements.
findings.quote: this amounted to a 6-db difference in the ratio of speech signal to background noise.

findings.antecedent: Speech intelligibility
findings.mechanism: The ability to understand intruding speech directly impacts the perception of privacy.
findings.quote: speech privacy is related to speech intelligibility.

findings.antecedent: Speech-to-noise ratio
findings.mechanism: Individuals establish a specific signal-to-noise ratio as their personal privacy threshold, with significant inter-subject variability.
findings.quote: each subject had a precise personal criterion for the speech-to-noise ratio which for him just constituted privacy, that there is a wide variation (10 db or so) in the criteria of various subjects

findings.antecedent: Background noise levels (varied)
findings.consequent: Tolerated speech levels (relative to noise, i.e., signal-to-noise ratio)
findings.mechanism: Subjects maintain a constant signal-to-noise ratio for their privacy threshold, regardless of absolute background noise level.
findings.quote: on the average our test subjects responded with a constant signal-to-noise ratio as the background levels varied.

findings.antecedent: Subject's criticality (least critical)
findings.mechanism: Individual differences in privacy sensitivity lead to varying tolerance for intruding speech.
findings.quote: the least critical subject allowed 20-db higher speech levels than the most critical.

findings.antecedent: Subject's definition of 'confidential' privacy
findings.mechanism: Individual differences in the interpretation of 'confidential' privacy lead to a 10 dB variation in tolerated speech levels.
findings.quote: When defining 'confidential' privacy, the maximum variation among subjects was about 10 db.

findings.antecedent: Privacy requirement (confidential vs. normal/everyday)
findings.consequent: Tolerated speech levels (for most critical subjects)
findings.mechanism: A higher privacy requirement (confidential) leads to a lower tolerance for intruding speech.
findings.quote: There was a shift of about 6 db between the definitions of 'normal' and 'confidential' privacy as given by the most critical subjects.

findings.antecedent: Wall type ('flat' wall with relatively weak low-frequency speech components)
findings.consequent: Tolerated articulation index (for critical and average subjects)
findings.mechanism: Subjects tolerated a higher AI for walls that transmitted speech with weak low-frequency components, suggesting a perceptual weighting of frequency content.
findings.quote: It appears that both the most critical 10% of the subjects and the average subject tolerated a higher articulation index for the 'flat' wall

findings.antecedent: Real or apparent intelligibility of intruding speech
findings.mechanism: The ability to understand or recognize speech is a primary driver of privacy judgments.
findings.quote: It is clear that real or apparent intelligibility is involved in the judgments of many if not most of them.

findings.antecedent: Beginning to understand intruding speech
findings.mechanism: The onset of intelligibility triggers a privacy-related reaction.
findings.quote: A typical comment was that the subject reacted when he could just begin to understand the intruding speech.

findings.antecedent: Intruding speech (distracting from work)
findings.mechanism: Intruding speech consumes cognitive resources, leading to distraction and annoyance.
findings.quote: Some of the less critical subjects said that they reacted when the intruding speech distracted them from the work

findings.antecedent: Speech sounds (recognizable as such, even with zero intelligibility)
findings.mechanism: Even gist perception or recognition of speech as speech, without full intelligibility, can trigger a privacy reaction.
findings.quote: Some of the most critical subjects appeared to react when the speech sounds became recognizable as such, even though the intelligibility of the speech was virtu-ally zero.

findings.antecedent: Intruding speech levels (clearly intelligible)
findings.mechanism: Individuals can maintain perceived privacy by adjusting their own behavior (e.g., lowering voice) even when intruding speech is intelligible.
findings.quote: One subject told us that even though the intruding speech levels were clearly intelligible, he knew that he could carry on a private conversation in his own office by the simple expedient of lowering his voice

findings.antecedent: Narrow (1/3 octave wide) 10-dB dip in TL curve
findings.mechanism: Narrow dips in TL are less perceptually salient and thus less important for overall annoyance, as predicted by AI.
findings.quote: a 10-db dip only one-third octave wide was judged to be relatively unimportant.

findings.antecedent: Contribution of TL dip to articulation index
findings.mechanism: The AI framework effectively predicts the perceptual importance of TL dips.
findings.quote: the importance was fairly well predicted by the contribution to the articulation index of the dip.

findings.antecedent: Narrow TL dip
findings.mechanism: The effect of narrow TL dips on annoyance is generally small and accounted for by the AI rating scheme.
findings.quote: the effect of a narrow TL dip is small, and, for the great majority of TL curves encountered, the effect is accounted for by the articulation-index rating scheme proposed here.

findings.antecedent: Deep dips in TL curve (low-frequency narrow bands of speech)
findings.mechanism: Very deep TL dips, especially at low frequencies, can cause annoyance not fully explained by speech intelligibility alone, suggesting other perceptual factors.
findings.quote: dips in the TL curve of a structure can, if they are deep enough, cause annoyance which is not explainable in terms of speech intelligibility.

findings.antecedent: Ratio of intruding speech to ambient/background noise
findings.mechanism: Privacy perception is primarily driven by the relative level of speech to noise, not the absolute speech level.
findings.quote: The typical test subject's feeling of privacy appears to be related to the ratio of the intruding speech to the ambient or background noise rather than to the level of the speech itself.

findings.antecedent: Articulation index (AI)
findings.mechanism: The AI, a weighted signal-to-noise ratio, correlates with subjective privacy reactions.
findings.quote: the subject reaction seems to be correlated with the articulation index which is a 'weighted' signal-to-noise ratio.

findings.antecedent: Articulation index (AI = 0.05)
findings.consequent: Feeling of lack of privacy (for most critical 10% of subjects)
findings.mechanism: An AI of 0.05 represents a threshold where critical individuals begin to perceive a lack of privacy.
findings.quote: the most critical 10% of the subjects began to feel a lack of privacy when the articulation index reached 0.05.

findings.antecedent: Articulation index (AI = 0.05)
findings.consequent: Perceived privacy (break point between adequate and inadequate 'confidential' privacy)
findings.mechanism: AI of 0.05 serves as a critical threshold for confidential privacy.
findings.quote: the most critical test subjects felt an AI of around 0.05 to be the 'break' point between adequate and inadequate 'confidential' privacy.

findings.antecedent: Articulation index (AI > 0.10) for 'everyday' privacy
findings.mechanism: A higher AI (lower privacy) is acceptable for 'everyday' privacy needs, even for critical individuals.
findings.quote: with 'everyday' privacy requirements, even the more critical subjects were satisfied with an AI somewhat greater than 0.10.

findings.antecedent: Total rating computed from proposed scheme (sum of 5 factors: source room size, speech use, background noise, noise reduction, privacy requirement)
findings.mechanism: The multi-factor rating scheme provides a good correlation with real-world occupant reactions to privacy.
findings.quote: The most significant fact about Fig. 20 is the fairly tight grouping of the data.

findings.antecedent: Proposed rating scheme (vs. average TL analysis)
findings.consequent: Correlation with observed subjective reaction to privacy
findings.mechanism: The proposed scheme, by incorporating multiple factors, offers a more accurate prediction of privacy satisfaction than average TL.
findings.quote: Certainly the grouping is much better than for the 'average TL' analysis which led to Fig. 1.

findings.antecedent: Articulation index (AI = 0.05)
findings.consequent: Perceived privacy (borderline between apparent satisfaction and some degree of dissatisfaction)
findings.mechanism: AI of 0.05 represents a critical threshold for overall privacy satisfaction.
findings.quote: situations with an articulation index of 0.05 are more or less on the borderline between apparent satisfaction and some degree of dissatisfaction.

findings.antecedent: Small change in noise reduction or background noise
findings.mechanism: The steep slope of the privacy rating curve indicates high sensitivity of occupant reaction to changes in acoustic parameters.
findings.quote: a small change in the noise reduction or background noise can make a significant variation in the occupant's reaction.

findings.antecedent: Increase in signal-to-noise ratio (10 dB or so) from AI=0.05
findings.mechanism: A relatively small increase in signal-to-noise ratio leads to a large increase in speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: an increase in the signal-to-noise ratio of only 10 or so db would be expected to result in fairly complete sentence intelligibility.

findings.antecedent: Occasional loud talker / raised voice
findings.mechanism: Occupants make allowances for occasional loud speech, adjusting their privacy expectations.
findings.quote: most occupants desire privacy on the average but may be willing to make allowances for the occasional loud talker and do not expect privacy when they themselves talk loudly.

findings.antecedent: Intelligibility of intruding speech sounds
findings.mechanism: Intelligibility is a primary determinant of perceived speech privacy.
findings.quote: Laboratory and field studies generally show a strong relationship between the intelligibility of intruding speech sounds and peoples' judgments of speech privacy.

findings.antecedent: Average TL values (as sole design parameter)
findings.mechanism: Average TL values are insufficient to capture the complex factors influencing speech privacy, leading to inaccurate design outcomes.
findings.quote: The use of average TL values as the sole parameter in designing for speech privacy can lead to grossly inaccurate results.

findings.antecedent: Proposed rating scheme (incorporating AI, background noise, room size, TL)
findings.mechanism: By integrating multiple factors that influence speech intelligibility, the proposed scheme provides a more accurate prediction of privacy.
findings.quote: The proposed scheme for designing for speech privacy and/or evaluating speech-privacy problems has proved to be more accurate because: (a) It rates the TL of sound-isolating structures according to their ability to reduce the intelligibility of intruding speech. (b) It recognizes the several other factors (such as background noise and room size) which combine with the TL to determine the intelligibility.

mechanisms: Masking of intruding speech sounds by steady background noise.
Speech intelligibility, as measured by the Articulation Index (AI), determines the perception of speech privacy.
Individual differences in personal criteria for acceptable speech-to-noise ratios.
Distraction from work due to intruding speech.
Recognition of speech sounds (even without full intelligibility) as a trigger for privacy judgments.
Behavioral adaptation (e.g., lowering one's voice) to maintain privacy in the presence of intelligible intruding speech.
moderators: Subject's criticality/individual differences in privacy sensitivity
Wall type/transmission loss (TL) curve shape (e.g., 'flat' vs. those with sharp dips)
Speech effort of the source talker (conversational, raised, loud voice)
implementation_implications: Design schemes for speech privacy should incorporate factors beyond average transmission loss, specifically considering speech intelligibility, background noise levels, room size, and speech effort.
An Articulation Index (AI) of 0.05 can serve as an economic design criterion for speech privacy, representing the borderline between satisfaction and dissatisfaction.
Small changes in noise reduction or background noise can lead to significant variations in occupant reactions to speech privacy, highlighting the importance of precise design.
Accurate prediction of background noise levels and the use of field-representative transmission loss data are crucial for effective speech privacy design.

Sound-power level (db re 10^-13 w) and importance function of normal speech in 1/3-octave and 1/2-octave bands.

Summary of case-history data, including description of space, construction, rating factors (source room size, speech use, background noise, noise reduction, privacy requirement), total rating, and observed reaction to privacy.

limitations: Studies were strictly limited to speech as the intruding signal, not other types of noise.
Laboratory studies were performed in the context of a typical office situation, limiting generalizability.

Field study and case histories were primarily from office situations, with limited data from hospitals, dormitories, and motels, requiring further verification for other space types (e.g., apartments).
Studies were restricted to buildings in the United States, and cultural differences might affect the average response curve.
The proposed rating scheme's overall uncertainty is estimated at ±4 or 5 db, requiring component accuracy of ±2 db.
Deep TL dips, especially at low frequencies, can cause annoyance not fully explained by speech intelligibility, indicating a limitation of the AI scheme in such specific cases.

paper_metadata.title: Speech Privacy in Buildings
paper_metadata.journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Obtaining adequate speech privacy in modern buildings is one of the important goals of the architect and consultant. This paper deals with the development of a rating method which takes into account the several factors influencing speech privacy. Our work in this area began with a brief laboratory study. The results indicated that speech privacy is related to speech intelligibility rather than to level. The initial experiments were supplemented with an analysis of about 40 case histories representing about 400 pairs of spaces in different kinds of buildings. There appears to be good correlation between the articulation index of intruding speech sound and the reactions of building occupants.
